title: Exif Clock Repair
user: People inheriting a large family-photo archive who need to understand and safely correct inconsistent capture times before sorting or sharing it.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A read-only external library of roughly 460k assets cannot complete metadata extraction reliably, leaving the owner unable to trust its catalog.
An archive owner investigates an eight-hour discrepancy across old photo timestamps after moving a family collection between Windows and macOS.

recurrence: Two 2025–26 reports at radically different scales; incorrect time ordering makes an archive hard to browse and creates risk of destructive bulk edits.
current_workaround: Run ExifTool commands by hand, compare file dates to EXIF fields in spreadsheets, and trial edits on copied folders.
incumbents_and_gap: ExifTool is powerful but exposes raw fields; Immich and Lightroom index metadata but are not a cautious explanation-and-repair workflow for conflicting timestamps.
smallest_useful_product: Offline desktop/PWA tool that scans a selected folder, groups date-field conflicts by likely timezone/camera pattern, previews a reversible sidecar patch, and exports a repair ledger. Non-goals: cloud backup, facial recognition, or changing pixels.
success_measure: In a pilot archive of 10k+ files, 80% of proposed corrections are accepted after spot checking and no unlogged metadata change is made.
monetization: one-time — episodic archive repair should not require uploading private family photos or maintaining a subscription.
constraints: Operate locally; never overwrite originals by default; preserve timezone provenance; write XMP/JSON sidecars before optional EXIF mutation; support only documented metadata formats.
why_distinct: It produces an auditable explanation and reversible repair plan, rather than being another photo manager or a thin wrapper around ExifTool.

title: Photo Metadata Inbox
user: Photographers with a large Lightroom-style library who need to progressively add captions and keywords without losing track of the untagged backlog.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A heavy tag user reports that the redesigned UI removed the ability to find untagged photos, even though the underlying search still works.
A Lightroom user says manually adding titles, captions, and keywords across large photo sets is very time-consuming and asks for tools that write IPTC fields.

recurrence: Two independent 2025–26 requests: finding the backlog and doing the enrichment both break down as libraries grow.
current_workaround: Use saved searches, bulk-select likely batches, and alternate between Lightroom/Immich panels and spreadsheets.
incumbents_and_gap: Lightroom, digiKam, and Immich store metadata; they do not make an offline, bounded queue with explicit completion and provenance the central artifact.
smallest_useful_product: Local web app that imports filenames, folders, and existing IPTC/XMP; presents a finite untagged queue by event; applies templates and controlled vocabulary; writes sidecars plus a change log. Non-goals: AI auto-captioning, DAM hosting, or replacing an editor.
success_measure: At least 60% of pilot users clear 500 previously untagged assets in 30 days while exporting a portable XMP change log.
monetization: one-time — private local catalog work has clear episodic value and should not charge per image.
constraints: No image upload; never silently overwrite IPTC fields; configurable vocabulary; preserve original sidecars and write atomic backups.
why_distinct: The product is a completion-oriented metadata work queue, not another general photo library or generative caption service.

title: Edit Portability Map
user: Photographers leaving Lightroom or using a read-only external library who need to know exactly which edits, dates, ratings, and metadata will travel safely.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A manually corrected capture date on an external-library video appears to save, then is reverted seconds later by the library workflow.
A photographer seeking a lower-resource, Linux-capable Lightroom alternative asks for current migration advice and describes unsatisfactory alternatives.

recurrence: Two current cross-tool ownership problems: edits can be overwritten, and a move requires guessing what is trapped in a catalog.
current_workaround: Export JPEGs, copy the catalog, search forum posts, and discover missing edits or metadata after switching applications.
incumbents_and_gap: Lightroom catalog export, darktable, and digiKam each cover parts of migration; none provides a neutral pre-flight inventory of portable versus app-local photo state.
smallest_useful_product: Read-only desktop CLI that inventories a Lightroom catalog/XMP and a target folder, classifies fields as embedded, sidecar, catalog-only, or target-unsupported, and produces a migration checklist and verification sample. Non-goals: converting RAW development recipes or modifying a live catalog.
success_measure: A user can inventory 95% of visible metadata/edit categories before migration and identify every catalog-only field in under 15 minutes.
monetization: one-time — migration planning is infrequent and users leaving a subscription service are sensitive to lock-in.
constraints: Read-only catalog access; document that proprietary edit recipes cannot be faithfully translated; do not ingest image pixels or cloud credentials.
why_distinct: It makes lock-in visible before a move instead of pretending to be a one-click Lightroom replacement.

title: RAW Fit Check
user: Photographers on older or modest computers who need to decide whether their camera RAW files will be viewable and workable before changing editors or hardware.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Nikon Z6II external library using embedded RAW previews displays an incorrect aspect ratio in web view, undermining confidence while evaluating a new photo system.
An owner of a Sony a6700 and a 2015 Mac asks which software can process the camera's RAW files when vendor software and current Lightroom are unsupported.

recurrence: Two 2025–26 compatibility failures at the camera/OS/editor boundary; the cost is buying or migrating before a basic viewing workflow is proven.
current_workaround: Install trial editors, search camera forums, and discover preview or decoder defects only after importing a real shoot.
incumbents_and_gap: Manufacturer compatibility lists and editor release notes are fragmented; photo managers report errors only after import and do not give a machine-specific preflight report.
smallest_useful_product: Local diagnostic that samples RAW files, extracts embedded previews and codec/camera identifiers, checks them against a transparent compatibility registry, and runs a tiny render/view benchmark. Non-goals: RAW editing, cloud conversion, or recommending hardware purchases.
success_measure: At least 90% of pilot users can classify a camera-file/editor-machine combination as usable, preview-only, or unsupported before importing a full shoot.
monetization: free — a transparent compatibility utility needs broad community contributions; paid support can follow if needed.
constraints: Registry claims must be versioned and evidence-backed; test files stay local; avoid reverse-engineering proprietary codecs beyond licensed libraries.
why_distinct: It tests a real file on the user's machine rather than serving another generic camera compatibility chart.

title: Ride Sensor Truth
user: Cyclists using wheel or cadence sensors who need a trustworthy record when the sensor silently disagrees with GPS during a ride.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A cyclist requests an alarm when a magnetic speed sensor drifts and reports a much lower speed than GPS; the current record uses only the bad sensor value.
A rider reports a cycle computer repeatedly stopping distance and speed recording mid-ride despite battery replacement and reset attempts.

recurrence: Separate sensor-failure reports show a common severity: a ride file can look plausible yet contain untrustworthy distance and speed.
current_workaround: Notice after the ride, inspect charts manually, re-seat a magnet, or choose GPS/sensor data globally with no incident record.
incumbents_and_gap: Strava, Garmin, and OpenTracks record activities, but their correction tools do not foreground a timestamped disagreement explanation and selectable data provenance.
smallest_useful_product: Offline FIT/GPX companion that compares GPS, wheel speed, cadence, and pauses; flags suspect segments; previews alternate totals; and exports a repaired copy plus provenance report. Non-goals: live navigation, hardware pairing, or social fitness feeds.
success_measure: On a labeled set of intentionally faulty rides, it identifies 90% of sustained sensor/GPS divergence events with fewer than one false alert per 10 ride-hours.
monetization: one-time — a privacy-preserving repair companion is used occasionally and has no need for a training-data subscription.
constraints: Keep route/location data local; never overwrite the original FIT/GPX; clearly label heuristic corrections; support only documented file formats.
why_distinct: It is a data-integrity and provenance layer, not a competing ride tracker.

title: Bike Service Receipts
user: Everyday cyclists maintaining one or more bikes who need a simple, evidence-backed record of what was done, what it cost, and what is next.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The requested service-history view explicitly needs per-bike filtering, action names, dates, costs, recent work, and a full scrollable history.
A new daily rider asks why and how often to maintain a dry chain, including consequences of not doing it systematically.

recurrence: One product backlog and one rider question converge on maintenance being both irregular and hard to recall; missing it risks wear and expensive replacement.
current_workaround: Keep receipts in a drawer, add vague phone reminders, or remember the last clean/lube/part change.
incumbents_and_gap: Strava tracks rides and bike-shop systems record their own jobs; generic maintenance apps rarely tie component evidence, cost, and mileage/time triggers into a portable receipt.
smallest_useful_product: Offline-first PWA with bike profiles, one-tap service receipts (actions, photo, cost, odometer), rule-based reminders, and CSV/PDF export. Non-goals: marketplace bookings, social sharing, or claiming to diagnose mechanical faults.
success_measure: After 60 days, 70% of pilot riders have logged three or more maintenance events and can answer the last-service date for every tracked component.
monetization: one-time — a personal maintenance log should remain usable without a cloud account.
constraints: Local storage/export first; reminders are informational, not safety certification; no medical or repair advice; users control all location/ride imports.
why_distinct: The primary artifact is a portable service receipt and next-action evidence, not another ride feed or bike-shop CRM.

title: Tour Route Intent
user: Self-supported touring cyclists who know the roads or paths they want but need a route file that preserves those deliberate choices across navigation apps.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A route planner keeps reconnecting waypoints onto an unwanted path; the requester wants it to preserve a known walking route between deliberate points.
A beginner asks what long-term bicycle tourists wish they knew about route planning, breakdowns, packing, budgets, and logistics.

recurrence: Route planning is a named concern for both a navigation user and prospective long-distance tourists; a wrong reroute can put a loaded rider onto unsuitable roads.
current_workaround: Add many waypoints, hand-draw a GPX in a desktop planner, and hope the phone app does not silently re-route during navigation.
incumbents_and_gap: Komoot, RideWithGPS, and Organic Maps plan routes well; they do not universally preserve the rider's rationale for an intentional detour, surface choice, or resupply constraint in a portable route artifact.
smallest_useful_product: Static web GPX planner that lets a user lock segments/waypoints and attach terse intent notes (surface, water, ferry, avoid-at-night), then validates whether an exported route still passes them. Non-goals: turn-by-turn navigation, live traffic, or map-data scraping.
success_measure: In a field test, 90% of exported routes retain every locked segment when imported into two target navigation apps.
monetization: one-time — route preparation is an occasional planning task and the export must remain usable without a hosted account.
constraints: Use openly licensed map tiles/data only; make routing-engine limitations explicit; no safety guarantee; location notes remain in the exported local file unless shared.
why_distinct: It protects deliberate route intent across tools rather than replacing a full navigation product.

title: Winter Ride Window
user: Commuter cyclists deciding whether a particular route is reasonably rideable in winter without turning vague weather anxiety into an all-or-nothing rule.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A navigator user asks for the screen to turn off automatically in navigation mode specifically to conserve energy, showing a concrete all-day-routing constraint.
A commuter asks for objective go/no-go criteria using temperature, ice risk, visibility, route type, and willingness to adapt their bike.

recurrence: A direct winter decision request plus a navigation battery constraint point to a need for short, practical pre-ride planning rather than another activity tracker.
current_workaround: Check several weather pages, make a subjective call, or avoid cycling for an entire season after a bad experience.
incumbents_and_gap: Weather apps forecast conditions and cycling maps show routes; neither turns selected user-defined limits and route exposure into a transparent, non-authoritative ride-window checklist.
smallest_useful_product: Static web planner where riders enter route exposure and personal thresholds, then receive a cited condition checklist, daylight/battery plan, and 'unknowns to check' rather than a safety verdict. Non-goals: live navigation, legal road-condition claims, or emergency advice.
success_measure: In a four-week winter pilot, users complete a pre-ride check in under two minutes and report fewer than 10% of completed rides as surprising relative to flagged conditions.
monetization: free — transparent safety-oriented planning is more credible without a conversion funnel; local sponsorship is optional later.
constraints: Use licensed forecast data; label uncertainty and never promise safety; retain no precise home/work route by default; country-specific rules must not be inferred.
why_distinct: It makes a rider's own limits explicit and auditable instead of issuing opaque, potentially unsafe 'ride/no ride' predictions.

title: Tabletop Match Ledger
user: Tabletop groups playing multi-round games with wraparound boards or cumulative scoring who need a shared, reliable match state between rounds.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A card-game product proposes first-class multi-hand matches because players otherwise repeatedly rematch and mentally add scores; it calls for persistent standings and a target.
A Stone Age player cannot track multiple hundreds on the board's 0–99 score track and asks for an intended or homebrew lap-count solution.

recurrence: Two independent tabletop contexts in the same week: multi-round totals and score-track wraparound force groups back to manual arithmetic.
current_workaround: Use paper, phone notes, a generic counter, or remember score laps separately from the game board.
incumbents_and_gap: BG Stats and generic score apps log plays, while individual games may provide score pads; a fast, no-account, round-aware shared ledger with explicit lap state is not their primary interaction.
smallest_useful_product: Local-network/offline PWA with a five-second setup, configurable players/rounds/score tracks, lap counters, target scoring, undo history, and a shareable final receipt. Non-goals: game rules enforcement, a BoardGameGeek clone, or public profiles.
success_measure: In 20 observed sessions, groups record every round without switching to paper and can resolve every disputed total from the immutable undo history.
monetization: one-time — a tabletop utility should keep working at a kitchen table with no account or recurring fee.
constraints: Offline/local-first synchronization; no copyrighted game assets or rules text; make all scoring formulas user-configurable rather than claiming official rules.
why_distinct: It models the state between rounds—laps, targets, and correction history—rather than being a generic numeric score pad.

title: Practice Loop Notebook
user: Instrumentalists learning a difficult few seconds from a recording who need deliberate looping with a written progression plan, not another streaming player.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A feature request says that without A–B repeat users must manually seek after every pass through a short passage, including for music practice.
A musician explicitly asks about practicing against deliberately fluctuating metronome timing, showing interest in specific, controlled practice constraints.

recurrence: One player feature request and one practice-method question show that the useful unit is a constrained passage and repeat plan, not a full song.
current_workaround: Manually seek in YouTube, use a metronome separately, and retain tempo/loop notes in memory or scattered notes.
incumbents_and_gap: Transcribe!, Amazing Slow Downer, and video players offer looping; they do not center a portable, per-passage deliberate-practice log with repetitions, tempo steps, and exit criteria.
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA that stores locally supplied audio/video references, A/B markers, a metronome ramp or variability plan, repetition counts, and a short reflection/export card. Non-goals: streaming-site downloading, copyrighted media hosting, or automated transcription.
success_measure: At least 50% of pilot musicians return to the same logged passage on three separate days and advance a recorded tempo or accuracy criterion.
monetization: one-time — musicians should be able to keep a personal practice archive without renting storage for their media.
constraints: Only reference or locally import user-controlled media; no platform scraping/download; audio processing stays in-browser; accessibility controls for tempo/click sounds.
why_distinct: It links looping to a repeatable practice decision and evidence trail, not just playback controls.

title: Solo Practice Bridge
user: Intermediate self-taught musicians who have lost regular teacher feedback and need a modest, non-AI plan that connects drills to pieces they actually want to play.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A guitar-practice system requests concrete modal practice examples that combine tonal context, fretboard position, ear cue, phrasing constraint, metronome, backing context, and a success cue.
After eight years with teachers and two years self-taught, a pianist reports a skill wall and difficulty practicing exercises outside pieces they enjoy.

recurrence: Independent guitar-system design and a pianist's direct account converge on the missing link between abstract drills and personally meaningful repertoire.
current_workaround: Follow generic exercise videos, maintain an ambitious practice list, or avoid drills and hope repertoire alone closes technique gaps.
incumbents_and_gap: Yousician, Simply Piano, and lesson marketplaces teach or assess; a transparent local planner for mapping a named piece problem to a small, self-authored drill loop is less served.
smallest_useful_product: Local web workbook with a repertoire goal, one observed obstacle, a timed drill/piece alternation, success cue, spaced revisit dates, and printable teacher-ready history. Non-goals: audio grading, generated lessons, subscriptions to a content catalog, or replacing a teacher.
success_measure: After four weeks, 60% of pilot users complete eight planned sessions and can name at least one drill-to-piece transfer they recorded.
monetization: one-time — the value is an enduring personal practice record, not a proprietary lesson stream.
constraints: No claims of pedagogical diagnosis; user enters all musical content; private by default; support accessibility-friendly timing and print export.
why_distinct: It scaffolds self-directed reflection and drill-to-repertoire transfer rather than wrapping a chatbot around music lessons.

title: Bird ID Evidence Card
user: Birders using an identification app who need to compare a tentative result against their own observed evidence before deciding whether to log it.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A BirdNET-Go user asks for typical song examples to compare with a detected bird, both for education and for checking possible false positives.
A birder says photos were too distant and Merlin was not definitive; nearby sound detections might belong to different birds, leaving an unresolved fulmar/kittiwake identification.

recurrence: Two 2026 sources identify the same trust gap: an automated suggestion is useful but insufficient when visual and audio evidence disagree or are weak.
current_workaround: Open multiple field-guide tabs, compare vague memories of calls, screenshot app suggestions, or record an uncertain sighting with no reasoning trail.
incumbents_and_gap: Merlin, BirdNET, and eBird provide identification and logging; they do not make a compact, user-owned comparison card that separates observed evidence from an algorithm's suggestion and preserves uncertainty.
smallest_useful_product: Offline-first mobile web form for recording date/location precision, visual traits, call notes, candidate species, confidence, and links to user-selected licensed reference recordings; export as a Markdown/CSV evidence card. Non-goals: species identification AI, copyrighted call library hosting, or a replacement citizen-science database.
success_measure: In a month-long pilot, 70% of uncertain sightings receive a complete evidence card and users report fewer unqualified 'certain' logs after later review.
monetization: free — conservation-adjacent logging benefits from portable data and trust; optional one-time export templates can fund maintenance.
constraints: Do not expose sensitive nesting locations by default; use only user-linked or openly licensed reference media; clearly distinguish suggestions from verified observations; respect eBird/BirdNET terms.
why_distinct: It improves calibration and provenance around an ID rather than offering another black-box identifier.
